entry.summary: I know. Another PDF API. Bear with me. The problem I kept running into Every time I needed HTML-to-PDF conversion in a project, I’d reach for one of the usual suspects: PDFShift, DocRaptor, API2PDF. They all work. They’re all reasonably well documented. PDFShift, for example, gives you 50 credits per month. Each credit covers a single conversion up to 5MB. entry.title: Automatically Generate ER Diagrams from SharePoint ERD Generator
entry.summary:
Generate ER Diagrams from SharePoint Lists – Introducing SharePoint ERD Generator
SharePoint is widely used as a lightweight data platform within Microsoft 365 environments. To address this, I built a browser extension called SharePoint ERD Generator. The extension collects metadata from lists in a SharePoint site and generates: PlantUML ER diagram code Excel-based table definitions (one sheet per list) Lookup relationship mappings Optional list filtering This allows you to quickly visualize and document list structures without manual diagram creation. Access the SharePoint site that contains the lists you want to document. Click SharePoint ERD Generator from your browser toolbar.
You can configure: Language (JP / EN) — reflected in UML output and Excel headers Column name style — Internal Name or Display Name Custom Excel columns — for example, adding a Notes or Description column Click Generate Diagram.
The extension will generate UML code and enable: Excel export
List filtering
PlantUML preview
Copying UML code to clipboard
Use Cases
Reviewing existing SharePoint-based systems Creating structured design documentation Performing impact analysis Preparing migration to Dataverse Improving governance and visibility Feedback and feature suggestions are welcome. Note: This article is based on a Japanese post originally published on Qiita and translated into English. https://qiita.com/reire/items/5c0d306a7cfc821ebda6

entry.title: JavaScript’s Weirdest Comparison
entry.summary:
[] == false // true [] == ![] // true
Wait… what? 🤯 How can an empty array be equal to false? JavaScript’s == operator performs type coercion. That means it tries to convert values to the same type before comparing them. [] == false
false becomes 0
[] becomes "" (empty string) "" becomes 0
So we end up with: 0 == 0 // true
[] == ![]
First evaluate ![]: [] is truthy ![] becomes false
So now we have: [] == false
Which we already know is: true
The == operator can lead to unexpected results because of implicit type conversion. That’s why most developers prefer: ===
It compares values without coercion. JavaScript doesn’t behave randomly. Understand coercion, and the weirdness disappears. Happy coding ✨

entry.title: What are Software Versions?
entry.summary:
I used to think software versions are consecutive numbers which change after every update. Why does something go from v1.1 to v1.2? The First Release
Imagine you and I build a simple app called TaskNest. v1.0.0 Semantic Versioning. A Bug Appears
The next day, someone reports: v1.0.1 v1.0.2 A Feature Grows
A week later, users ask: v1.1.0 v1.2.0 The Big Decision
Months pass. The app grows. v2.0.0 And That’s It Last number → small fix Middle number → new feature First number → breaking change It’s not random. When you see v2.1.3, you’re not just seeing numbers. “How much did I change the story?”
